blocks.content: With concurrency and parallelism now clearly distinguished, this chapter covers the two concrete implementation choices a real program has for actually achieving either one: multithreading, running several threads inside one process, or multiprocessing, running several fully separate processes. Both can achieve concurrency, and both can achieve genuine parallelism on suitable hardware, but they make very different tradeoffs to get there.

This chapter is deliberately a direct comparison built entirely on material already covered in depth elsewhere in this course, the threads in Linux module for multithreading mechanics, and the fork chapter plus the shared memory and IPC modules for multiprocessing mechanics, rather than introducing new low level mechanisms from scratch.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199370-848924406.png
1. The Core Structural Difference

Multithreading means running multiple threads inside a single process, all sharing that process one address space, exactly as covered in full in the threads in Linux module, code, heap, and open files shared, only the stack and register state private to each thread. Multiprocessing instead means running multiple genuinely separate processes, each with its own completely independent address space, created via fork and exec exactly as covered in that dedicated chapter.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199370-725399697.png
2. Crash Isolation: A Real, Practical Consequence
blocks.text: 2. Crash Isolation: A Real, Practical Consequence

blocks.content: This structural difference has a genuinely important practical consequence for reliability. Because threads share one address space, a serious bug in one thread, corrupting shared memory or crashing outright, can bring down the entire process, every single thread included, with no isolation between them at all.

Separate processes under multiprocessing do not share an address space, so a crash in one process is naturally contained, it does not directly corrupt or crash its sibling processes, which keep running completely unaffected. This is exactly why genuinely critical, fault tolerant systems often deliberately choose multiprocessing specifically for this isolation property, even at some real communication cost.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199370-577338570.png
blocks.alt: Crash Isolation: A Real, Practical Consequence

blocks.title: A real world consequence worth knowing
blocks.content: Many web browsers deliberately run each tab as a separate process specifically for this reason, a single misbehaving or crashing tab does not bring down the entire browser and every other open tab along with it.
3. Communication Cost

Threads within one process communicate essentially for free, through the shared heap they already share by default, no copying, no kernel mediation, no explicit IPC mechanism required at all, exactly the shared memory advantage covered in the shared memory chapter, just automatic rather than something that needs to be deliberately set up.

Separate processes under multiprocessing have no such automatic sharing, they need a real, explicit IPC mechanism, a pipe, a socket, a deliberately created shared memory segment, every one covered in full in the IPC module, and every one carrying real, measurable overhead compared to a thread simply reading a shared variable directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199370-173319939.png

4. Creation Cost

Creating a new thread is comparatively lightweight, it shares the existing process address space entirely, needing only a new stack and a new kernel scheduling entry, exactly as covered in the threads in Linux module. Creating a new process via fork is heavier, since it needs to set up a genuinely separate address space, though the copy on write technique from the fork chapter substantially reduces this real cost in practice by deferring actual memory duplication until a write genuinely happens.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199371-156399678.png
5. Both Can Achieve True Parallelism, With a Condition
blocks.text: 5. Both Can Achieve True Parallelism, With a Condition

blocks.content: Directly applying the previous chapter distinction, neither multithreading nor multiprocessing automatically guarantees genuine parallelism just by existing. Both only actually achieve true, simultaneous parallel execution if the underlying system genuinely has multiple CPU cores AND the scheduler actually places the different threads or processes onto separate cores to run at the exact same instant.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199371-402206944.png
blocks.alt: Both Can Achieve True Parallelism, With a Condition

blocks.content: 6. A Real, Important Caveat: The Python GIL
blocks.text: 6. A Real, Important Caveat: The Python GIL

blocks.content: The threads in Linux module already flagged this briefly, and it deserves a full, direct treatment here, precisely because it is a genuinely common, practical reason to choose multiprocessing over multithreading despite multithreading normally lower overhead. CPython, the standard Python implementation, has a Global Interpreter Lock that only allows one thread to execute Python bytecode at any given instant, even on a machine with many available CPU cores.

This means multithreading in standard Python cannot achieve genuine CPU bound parallelism no matter how many cores are available, the GIL structurally prevents it. Multiprocessing genuinely sidesteps this limitation entirely, since each separate process gets its own fully independent Python interpreter and therefore its own independent GIL, allowing real, measurable parallel speedup for CPU bound Python work that pure multithreading simply cannot deliver.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199842-452884822.png
blocks.alt: A Real, Important Caveat: The Python GIL

7. Choosing Between Them in Practice

A practical decision guide follows directly from everything covered in this chapter. Work that needs fast, frequent access to shared state, and where the overhead of thread creation and shared memory access genuinely matters, favors multithreading. Work that needs strong crash isolation, or that needs to sidestep a limitation like the Python GIL, favors multiprocessing, accepting its real communication overhead in exchange.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785419199843-726632438.png
8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Assuming multithreading is always the right, faster choice simply because it has lower overhead, without weighing crash isolation or a real constraint like the Python GIL that specifically favors multiprocessing instead.","Forgetting that neither multithreading nor multiprocessing automatically guarantees true parallelism, both still require genuinely multiple cores actually scheduled to run work simultaneously.","Not being able to explain concretely why the Python GIL specifically motivates choosing multiprocessing over multithreading for CPU bound work, a genuinely common, practical interview question."]
items: Assuming multithreading is always the right, faster choice simply because it has lower overhead, without weighing crash isolation or a real constraint like the Python GIL that specifically favors multiprocessing instead.
Forgetting that neither multithreading nor multiprocessing automatically guarantees true parallelism, both still require genuinely multiple cores actually scheduled to run work simultaneously.
Not being able to explain concretely why the Python GIL specifically motivates choosing multiprocessing over multithreading for CPU bound work, a genuinely common, practical interview question.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to compare multithreading and multiprocessing precisely along communication cost, creation cost, and crash isolation, and to explain the Python GIL as a concrete, real world example of why multiprocessing sometimes genuinely beats multithreading despite its higher overhead.

With multithreading and multiprocessing compared directly, the next chapter turns to thread safety, the discipline of writing code that behaves correctly when multiple threads genuinely do share state, tying directly back to the synchronization module.
